lesson_title: Nine Metres of Tube: Where Your Food Really Goes
hook_text: The food in your stomach is not inside your body yet. Here is when it finally gets in.
clip_script: Your body is a tube with you wrapped around it, mouth to anus, about nine metres if you stretched it out. Food in that tube is not truly inside you yet. Follow one bite of pap and beans. Mouth: teeth chop, saliva wets, and already a chemical starts turning starch into sugar. Swallow, and rings of muscle squeeze it down the gullet, peristalsis, which is why you can swallow upside down. Stomach: a washing machine full of acid, churning for hours into a thick soup. Then the small intestine, six metres long, lined with millions of tiny fingers called villi. Juices from the liver and pancreas finish breaking the food into pieces so small they dissolve, and they cross the wall into your blood. Now, finally, the food is inside you. What is left is fibre you cannot digest. The large intestine squeezes the water out of it and pushes the rest out. Take it in, break it down, soak it up, use it, push out the rest.
visual_style: A see-through body with a glowing tube; a bite of food travels as a dot, squeezed by muscle rings, churned in a bag, then crossing finger-like villi into red blood vessels; five verbs stamp across the screen at the end.
pacing: Hook pause, a steady journey down the tube, a dramatic beat as food crosses into the blood, a five-verb finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and name the five processes in order.
